readme:
FULL-STACK DEVELOPER 2026
Phase 17 - Supabase Authentication
Volume 05 - Authentication & Security

This phase implements Supabase Auth in the existing Next.js App Router application using the current SSR cookie model. It intentionally stops before NestJS bearer-token verification; that is Phase 18.

Locked additions:
- @supabase/supabase-js 2.116.0
- @supabase/ssr 0.12.7

Start with 00_Phase_17_Guide.pdf or 12_Phase_17_Complete_Book.pdf.

lessons.body:
Supabase Auth Architecture & Keys
Place identity, sessions, keys, Next.js, and NestJS in the correct security boundaries

Phase 17 - Supabase Authentication
Volume 05 - Authentication & Security

Architecture milestone

Supabase Auth

v

Next.js session

v

NestJS later verifies bearer token

v

Business authorization remains separate

Phase 17 implements cookie-based Supabase Auth in Next.js. NestJS token verification remains Phase 18.

Supabase Auth is the identity provider, not the application
backend
TaskFlow already has a NestJS backend that owns application rules and Prisma persistence. Supabase Auth is
introduced to establish identity and manage the authentication session. It does not replace TasksService,
authorization rules, or the NestJS API.

Figure 1 - Responsibility split

Supabase Auth: credentials + session + access token

v

Next.js: web session and authenticated pages

v

NestJS (Phase 18): verify bearer token

v

Service layer: ownership, membership, permissions

v

Prisma/PostgreSQL: durable business data

Authentication and business authorization remain separate layers.

Concern                                             Owner in TaskFlow

Password verification / email confirmation          Supabase Auth

Cookie-backed SSR session                           Next.js + @supabase/ssr

JWT verification for protected API                  NestJS guard in Phase 18

Task ownership / Workspace permission               NestJS service/authorization layer

Business records                                    Prisma + PostgreSQL

Why two Supabase packages?
@supabase/supabase-js is the base SDK. @supabase/ssr wraps it for frameworks where the same authenticated
session must be readable on the browser and server through cookies. Current Supabase guidance recommends
@supabase/ssr for Next.js cookie-backed sessions.

Publishable key vs secret key
The Project URL and Publishable key are intentionally used by the browser-facing client. A service-role or secret key
has elevated privileges and must never be placed in NEXT_PUBLIC_* variables, browser bundles, or source
examples.

Do not confuse the key with the user

A public/publishable project key identifies the Supabase project/client capability. The signed-in user identity still comes from
the authenticated session and verified access token.

lessons.summary: Dashboard URLs, Email Confirmation & SSR Flow Configure the identity provider so the code has a correct redirect and confirmation environment Phase 17 - Supabase Authentication Volume 05 - Authentication & Security Architecture milestone Signup v Confirmation email v Server confirmation route v Session established…
lessons.body:
Dashboard URLs, Email Confirmation &
SSR Flow
Configure the identity provider so the code has a correct redirect and confirmation environment

Phase 17 - Supabase Authentication
Volume 05 - Authentication & Security

Architecture milestone

Signup

v

Confirmation email

v

Server confirmation route

v

Session established

Phase 17 implements cookie-based Supabase Auth in Next.js. NestJS token verification remains Phase 18.

Configure Auth before writing UI code
Authentication flows depend on dashboard configuration. If the Site URL or email template is wrong, perfectly correct
Next.js code can still redirect to the wrong place or fail to establish an SSR session.

Local development configuration
• Keep the Email provider enabled.

• Use email confirmation for the production-style learning flow.

• Set Site URL to http://localhost:3000 during local development.

• Add staging and production URLs to the allowed redirect list before deployment.

• Do not weaken confirmation or redirect policy merely to make testing easier.

SSR confirmation email template
For the server-rendered PKCE-style flow used here, the confirmation email sends a token hash back to a server route
that exchanges it for a session cookie.

{{ .SiteURL }}/auth/confirm?token_hash={{ .TokenHash }}&type=email

Figure 1 - Email confirmation

User submits signup

v

Supabase creates pending user

v

Email contains token_hash link

v

Browser opens /auth/confirm

v

Route calls verifyOtp(token_hash)

v

Supabase establishes session

v

Cookies written

v

Redirect to /account

The token hash is exchanged server-side; the authenticated session is then stored through the SSR cookie client.

Redirect URLs are security configuration

Do not allow arbitrary destinations from user-controlled next parameters without validating same-origin/relative paths. This
phase uses a fixed /account destination to keep the flow explicit.

lessons.summary: Next.js 16 Proxy, Session Refresh & getClaims Keep SSR cookies synchronized and verify identity at the request boundary Phase 17 - Supabase Authentication Volume 05 - Authentication & Security Architecture milestone Browser cookies v Proxy v getClaims v Protected route Phase 17 implements cookie-based Supabase…
lessons.body:
Next.js 16 Proxy, Session Refresh &
getClaims
Keep SSR cookies synchronized and verify identity at the request boundary

Phase 17 - Supabase Authentication
Volume 05 - Authentication & Security

Architecture milestone

Browser cookies

v

Proxy

v

getClaims

v

Protected route

Phase 17 implements cookie-based Supabase Auth in Next.js. NestJS token verification remains Phase 18.

Next.js 16 uses Proxy for the request boundary
Next.js renamed Middleware to Proxy in version 16. Supabase relies on this request boundary because Server
Components cannot reliably write refreshed auth cookies themselves.

Figure 1 - Proxy refresh path

Browser sends auth cookies

v

proxy.ts runs

v

createServerClient reads cookies

v

getClaims verifies/refreshes access token

v

request cookies updated

v

response Set-Cookie updated

v

Server Component renders with synchronized session

Proxy keeps browser and server session state synchronized.

Why getClaims belongs here
Current Supabase guidance says to use getClaims when protecting pages and user data. It verifies the access token
signature against the project JWKS when asymmetric signing keys are used, and it refreshes a session that is near
expiry.

Do not protect SSR pages with getSession().user

getSession reads session storage but does not itself revalidate the stored user identity. Use getClaims for verified identity, or
getUser when a fresh Auth-server user record is required.

Public vs protected paths
TaskFlow protects /account and /tasks in this phase. /login and /auth/* remain public so users can establish or repair
authentication. Phase 19 will add authorization beyond mere signed-in status.

function isProtectedPath(pathname: string) {
return pathname.startsWith('/account') ||
pathname.startsWith('/tasks')
}

const { data, error } = await supabase.auth.getClaims()
const authenticated = !error && Boolean(data?.claims)

if (isProtectedPath(request.nextUrl.pathname) && !authenticated) {
// redirect to /login
}

lessons.title: Signup and Email Confirmation
lessons.summary: Signup & Email Confirmation Handle pending confirmation explicitly and exchange the email token hash for a session Phase 17 - Supabase Authentication Volume 05 - Authentication & Security Architecture milestone signUp v Pending confirmation v verifyOtp v Authenticated session Phase 17 implements cookie-based Supabase Auth…
lessons.body:
Signup & Email Confirmation
Handle pending confirmation explicitly and exchange the email token hash for a session

Phase 17 - Supabase Authentication
Volume 05 - Authentication & Security

Architecture milestone

signUp

v

Pending confirmation

v

verifyOtp

v

Authenticated session

Phase 17 implements cookie-based Supabase Auth in Next.js. NestJS token verification remains Phase 18.

Signup is not always immediate login
With email confirmation enabled, signUp can create the user while returning no active session. The UI must represent
this as a pending-confirmation state rather than assuming signup always means the user is already authenticated.

Figure 1 - Signup state machine

Submit email + password

v

signUp()

v

Error? -> generic signup failure

v

No session? -> ask user to check email

v

Confirmation link -> verifyOtp

v

Session established

v

Redirect to /account

Email confirmation is part of the authentication lifecycle, not an unrelated email feature.

const { data, error } = await supabase.auth.signUp({
email,
password,
})

if (error) {
redirect('/login?error=Unable+to+create+account')
}

if (!data.session) {
redirect('/login?message=Check+your+email+to+confirm+your+account')
}

redirect('/account')

Confirmation endpoint
The /auth/confirm route reads token_hash and type, verifies the OTP/token hash with Supabase Auth, allows the
server client to persist the session cookies, then redirects to the authenticated area. Keep public signup/sign-in
failures generic because auth systems may deliberately avoid exposing whether an account exists.

const { error } = await supabase.auth.verifyOtp({
type,
token_hash: tokenHash,
})

if (!error) return NextResponse.redirect(accountUrl)

lessons.summary: Sign-In, Sign-Out & Session Lifecycle Create and terminate real Supabase sessions without confusing UI state with security state Phase 17 - Supabase Authentication Volume 05 - Authentication & Security Architecture milestone Sign in v Cookie session v Authenticated use v Local sign out Phase 17…
lessons.body:
Sign-In, Sign-Out & Session Lifecycle
Create and terminate real Supabase sessions without confusing UI state with security state

Phase 17 - Supabase Authentication
Volume 05 - Authentication & Security

Architecture milestone

Sign in

v

Cookie session

v

Authenticated use

v

Local sign out

Phase 17 implements cookie-based Supabase Auth in Next.js. NestJS token verification remains Phase 18.

Sign-in establishes the cookie-backed session
TaskFlow uses a Server Action to submit email/password to Supabase Auth. When authentication succeeds,
@supabase/ssr writes the session into cookies through the server client/response path.

const { error } = await supabase.auth.signInWithPassword({
email,
password,
})

if (error) {
redirect('/login?error=Unable+to+sign+in')
}

revalidatePath('/', 'layout')
redirect('/account')

Why the public error is generic
Supabase sign-in errors can intentionally avoid distinguishing a missing account from a wrong password. TaskFlow
preserves that privacy behavior instead of displaying account-enumeration hints.

Sign-out scope is a product decision
Supabase JavaScript signOut supports global, local, and others scopes. JavaScript defaults to global. TaskFlow
explicitly chooses local for the ordinary Sign out button so one browser session does not unexpectedly terminate the
user on every other device.

await supabase.auth.signOut({ scope: 'local' })

Scope                            Meaning

local                            Terminate the current session only

global                           Terminate all refresh sessions for the user

others                           Terminate other sessions while keeping current session

Access-token nuance

Revoking/signing out refresh-session state does not magically invalidate an already issued access token before its exp time.
This is why short access-token lifetimes and server verification still matter.

lessons.summary: Protected Server Components & Authenticated UI Render authenticated pages from verified request identity, not client-side guesses Phase 17 - Supabase Authentication Volume 05 - Authentication & Security Architecture milestone Request v Proxy v getClaims v Server Component Phase 17 implements cookie-based Supabase Auth in Next.js.…
lessons.body:
Protected Server Components & Authenticated UI Render authenticated pages from verified request identity, not client-side guesses Phase 17 - Supabase Authentication Volume 05 - Authentication & Security Architecture milestone Request v Proxy v getClaims v Server Component Phase 17 implements cookie-based Supabase Auth in Next.js. NestJS token verification remains Phase 18. A protected page must verify the request, not trust presentation state Hiding a navigation link is not route protection. The request boundary and/or Server Component must derive authenticated identity from the verified session. export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic' export default async function AccountPage() { const supabase = await createClient() const { data, error } = await supabase.auth.getClaims() if (error || !data?.claims) { redirect('/login') } return

Subject: {String(data.claims.sub)}

} Figure 1 - Defense in depth for a protected page Request enters Proxy v Proxy refreshes/verifies session v Unauthenticated protected request redirects v Server Component calls getClaims v Verified claims used for identity-aware rendering The page does not trust a client-side loggedIn boolean. When getUser is useful getClaims verifies the access token efficiently. getUser performs a network request to Supabase Auth and returns the most current user record. Use it when fresh account state matters enough to pay the network cost, such as security-sensitive session state or user-profile data that may have changed at the provider. Authenticated UI state is not authorization A page may show the authenticated email or subject, but this does not yet decide which Workspace or Task the user can access. That becomes Phase 19 authorization and ownership.

getClaims, getUser, getSession & API
Token Handoff
Use each Supabase Auth method for its intended trust job and prepare the NestJS boundary

Phase 17 - Supabase Authentication
Volume 05 - Authentication & Security

Architecture milestone

Verified claims

v

Fresh user record

v

Raw session/token

v

NestJS handoff

Phase 17 implements cookie-based Supabase Auth in Next.js. NestJS token verification remains Phase 18.

Three Auth methods, three jobs
Current Supabase SSR guidance distinguishes getClaims, getUser, and getSession. Using each for the correct
reason prevents subtle trust bugs.

Method                        Use when                                         Trust note

getClaims()                   Protect pages/data; verify JWT identity          Verifies token signature/claims; preferred for SSR
protection

getUser()                     Need fresh user record from Auth server          Network request; catches account/session state
changes

getSession()                  Need raw access/refresh token or expiry          Do not trust embedded user by itself in server cookie
context

Phase 18 handoff: forwarding the access token
TaskFlow has a separate NestJS API. To call it, Next.js will eventually need the raw access token. getSession is
appropriate for retrieving the token as transport material, but Next.js must not treat the session.user object as the final
authorization proof.

const {
data: { session },
} = await supabase.auth.getSession()

const accessToken = session?.access_token

// Phase 18:
// Authorization: Bearer <accessToken>
// NestJS verifies it before trusting sub/claims.

Transport is not trust

Next.js retrieving an access token does not make NestJS trust it. Phase 18 creates the verification boundary in the API.

Revocation gap
A correctly signed, unexpired access token can remain valid until exp even after the underlying refresh session is
revoked. The Supabase advanced guide recommends getUser where detecting server-side session termination
immediately matters. This is a product/security policy choice, not a reason to call getUser on every render
automatically.

lessons.body:
SSR Caching, Refresh & Auth Debugging
Diagnose session failures without weakening cookie or token security

Phase 17 - Supabase Authentication
Volume 05 - Authentication & Security

Architecture milestone

Cookie synchronization

v

Refresh

v

Cache boundaries

v

Debug evidence

Phase 17 implements cookie-based Supabase Auth in Next.js. NestJS token verification remains Phase 18.

SSR authentication fails in ways ordinary client-only auth does not
Cookie synchronization, token refresh, route prefetching, caching, and response headers all affect SSR
authentication. Random logout symptoms often come from session cookies not being propagated consistently.

Symptom                                                First layer to inspect

User signs in then appears logged out on Server        Proxy/session-cookie refresh path
Component

Works client-side, fails server-side                   server.ts cookies + Proxy

Confirmation returns to wrong host                     Supabase Site URL / redirect configuration

Repeated random logout                                 Proxy response/cookies being replaced incorrectly

One user receives another session                      CDN/ISR caching authenticated response - critical

getSession has user but protected page should reject   Use getClaims/getUser for identity verification

Do not cache authenticated Set-Cookie responses publicly
Supabase warns that session refresh writes Set-Cookie. If a CDN caches that response and serves it to another
visitor, session leakage can occur. Current @supabase/ssr versions provide cache-related headers during refresh;
the Proxy must apply those headers. Authenticated routes should not use ISR casually.

Next.js route prefetching

Authentication flows that depend on a browser first processing new cookies can interact poorly with prefetching. Keep the SSR
guide current, test real navigation behavior, and use dynamic rendering for authenticated pages when request-time session
state is required.

Debug with observable boundaries
• Confirm NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL and publishable key are loaded in apps/web.

• Confirm the dashboard Site URL matches the browser origin.

• Inspect the /auth/confirm request and redirect chain.

• Inspect Set-Cookie responses without copying token values into logs/screenshots.

• Confirm proxy.ts matcher actually runs for protected routes.

• Confirm getClaims returns verified claims after sign-in/refresh.

• Do not fix auth by disabling cookie security or exposing a secret key.

lessons.body:
Security Boundaries & NestJS Handoff
Define exactly what Phase 17 protects and what remains untrusted until Phase 18

Phase 17 - Supabase Authentication
Volume 05 - Authentication & Security

Architecture milestone

Next.js authenticated session

v

Access token transport

v

NestJS verification next

v

Authorization later

Phase 17 implements cookie-based Supabase Auth in Next.js. NestJS token verification remains Phase 18.

Phase 17 stops at the web-session boundary
The user can now authenticate to Supabase and maintain a Next.js SSR session. The NestJS API is not protected
yet. Keeping this boundary explicit prevents a dangerous illusion that a protected page automatically means a
protected backend.

Figure 1 - Current vs next phase

Phase 17: Supabase Auth session established

v

Next.js obtains access token when needed

v

Phase 18: send Authorization Bearer token to NestJS

v

NestJS verifies token

v

Trusted authenticated user attached to request

v

Phase 19: ownership/RBAC authorization

Authentication is built layer by layer instead of trusting the browser.

What may be browser-visible
Value                                                      Browser-visible?

Supabase Project URL                                       Yes

Supabase Publishable key                                   Yes

Access token                                               Credential - browser/session system may possess it; never log it

Refresh token                                              Highly sensitive session credential; never log/expose intentionally

Supabase Secret / service-role key                         Never

DATABASE_URL                                               Never

Do not use the database Auth schema as application authorization logic
Supabase Auth maintains identity information in its auth schema. TaskFlow still has its own domain User,
Membership, Workspace, Project, and Task records. Phase 19 will establish the explicit link from verified auth subject
to application authorization data.

RLS boundary

Supabase RLS is crucial when browser clients call Supabase Data APIs directly. TaskFlow business data currently flows
through NestJS + Prisma instead. We will not introduce duplicate authorization systems without a concrete reason.

API

Phase 17 - Supabase Authentication
Volume 05 - Authentication & Security

Architecture milestone

Configure

v

Sign up

v

Confirm

v

v

v

Phase 17 implements cookie-based Supabase Auth in Next.js. NestJS token verification remains Phase 18.

Hands-on lab: make authentication observable
Complete the lab in order. Do not proceed because the login page looks correct; proceed because each session
transition is verified.

Lab A - Install and configure
• From taskflow\apps\web install @supabase/supabase-js@2.116.0 and @supabase/ssr@0.12.7.

• Create .env.local from .env.local.example using your project URL and Publishable key.

• Configure Site URL and the signup confirmation template in the Supabase dashboard.

• Create browser.ts/server.ts equivalents and proxy.ts exactly once - do not create duplicate auth clients per feature.

Lab B - Verify flows
Test                                                          Expected result

Open /account signed out                                      Redirect to /login

Create account with confirmation enabled                      Message asks you to check email; no false authenticated UI

Open confirmation email                                       /auth/confirm verifies token hash and redirects to /account

Refresh /account repeatedly                                   Session remains valid; no random logout

Sign out                                                      Current session ends; protected page redirects again

Use invalid/expired confirmation link                         Safe auth error page

Lab C - Explain the trust chain
Draw this without looking at the book: Credentials -> Supabase Auth -> cookie-backed session -> Proxy/getClaims ->
verified claims -> protected Next.js page -> raw access token when calling NestJS -> NestJS verification in Phase 18.

Exercise levels
Level                         Challenge

1 - Follow                    Reproduce the reference auth flow and verify every transition.

2 - Modify                    Add a public /about route while keeping /account and /tasks protected. Explain where the rule belongs.

3 - Implement                 Add a "Sign out all devices" action that intentionally uses global scope and clearly labels the effect.

4 - Engineer                  Design an HRIS login/session policy: email confirmation, MFA trigger, local vs global logout, fresh-user checks
for payroll approval, and session-revocation expectations.

Phase exit checklist
• You can explain why @supabase/ssr exists in addition to supabase-js.

• You know which Supabase values may be NEXT_PUBLIC and which must never be public.

• You can implement the browser client, server client, and Next.js 16 Proxy session path.

• You use getClaims for protected SSR identity checks rather than trusting getSession().user.

• You can explain email confirmation token-hash exchange.

• You can explain local vs global sign out.

• You understand why authenticated responses must not be cached across users.

• You can retrieve an access token for transport to NestJS without treating it as verified by NestJS.

• You understand that Phase 17 authenticates the web session but does not yet secure the NestJS API.

Figure 1 - Phase 17 exit architecture

Credentials

v

Supabase Auth

v

SSR cookie session

v

Next.js Proxy + getClaims

v

Protected Next.js UI

v

Access token ready for API transport

v

Phase 18 NestJS verification

Phase 17 is complete when the web session works reliably and the learner can explain every trust boundary.

Before you touch the code

Architecture trace
auth form -> Supabase Auth -> session/cookies -> Next.js server/client auth helpers -> protected UI -> access token handoff

lessons.title: Debugging Workshop
lessons.summary:
Goal
Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it.
lessons.body:
Debugging Workshop — Phase 17: Supabase Authentication

Goal
Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it.

The debugging loop
1. Reproduce the failure with the smallest reliable action.
2. Capture the exact symptom: command, status code, stack trace, network request, database state, or UI state.
3. Locate the earliest boundary where actual behavior diverges from expected behavior.
4. Form one hypothesis.
5. Change one variable.
6. Re-run the same reproduction.
7. Keep the fix only if the evidence supports the hypothesis.

Boundary walk
auth form -> Supabase Auth -> session/cookies -> Next.js server/client auth helpers -> protected UI -> access token handoff

Start at the visible symptom and walk backward. Do not debug the database when the browser never sent the request. Do not debug React state when the API is returning a deterministic 403. The boundary walk tells you which evidence to collect next.

Failure drill 1 — Using service-role key in browser code
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

lessons.title: Phase Synthesis & Independent Challenge
lessons.summary:
Mission
Rebuild the capability of Phase 17 without following the exact code line-by-line. The goal is transfer: can you use the ideas when the variable names, UI, or route shape changes?
lessons.body:
Phase Synthesis & Independent Challenge — Supabase Authentication

Mission
Rebuild the capability of Phase 17 without following the exact code line-by-line. The goal is transfer: can you use the ideas when the variable names, UI, or route shape changes?

Required outcome
Integrate Supabase Auth into Next.js with correct browser/server clients, cookie/session behavior, sign-up/sign-in/sign-out, and protected routing.

Required artifact
Working TaskFlow authentication UI/session integration whose server-side checks are explicit and ready to hand tokens to NestJS.

Constraints
• Start from the previous phase checkpoint or a fresh branch.
• Use the course architecture boundaries, but do not copy the reference implementation until after your first attempt.
• Keep changes scoped to the capability.
• Preserve validation, authorization, error handling, and observability expectations already earned in earlier phases.
• Record any design decision where more than one implementation is reasonable.

Acceptance criteria
• Can distinguish public and secret Supabase keys.
• Can create browser/server clients.
• Can explain cookie/session flow.
• Can prepare a verified API handoff.

Independent build sequence
1. Configure project URLs/redirects and explain why local/preview/production values differ.
2. Create browser and server Supabase clients with the correct key exposure model.
3. Implement sign-up/sign-in and surface provider errors safely.
4. Render authenticated state on the server rather than trusting only client state.
5. Implement sign-out and prove protected routes recover to unauthenticated state.
6. Inspect the session/access token and prepare the boundary for NestJS verification without exposing service-role credentials.

Self-review
Compare your implementation to the reference only after the acceptance criteria pass. Differences are not automatically mistakes. For each difference, ask: does it preserve the same contract, security boundary, correctness, maintainability, and operational behavior? Keep the alternative when you can justify it with evidence.

Stretch challenge
Change one assumption: more users, a second tenant, a slow network, an expired session, a concurrent mutation, a deployment restart, or a failed dependency. Predict whether your design still behaves correctly. If not, document the next architectural improvement rather than adding complexity blindly.

Phase exit
Run the relevant checks, inspect Git diff, and write a three-sentence summary: what the system can do now, which boundary owns the new responsibility, and which failure you now know how to diagnose. Only then mark the phase complete.

lessons.title: Mastery Capstone Lab
lessons.summary: Integrate Phase 17 without following a transcript.
lessons.body:
Mastery Capstone Lab

This is the transfer exercise for Phase 17: Supabase Authentication. The detailed lessons are now closed-book reference material. Your task is to prove that the phase outcome can be reproduced from requirements, repository evidence, and debugging—not by copying a finished implementation.

Target artifact
Working TaskFlow authentication UI/session integration whose server-side checks are explicit and ready to hand tokens to NestJS.

Acceptance criteria
- Write the behavior and constraints before implementation.
- Identify the owning layer and every boundary crossed.
- Implement the smallest complete vertical slice.
- Verify the happy path from outside the implementation.
- Demonstrate at least one expected failure path.
- Run the phase-relevant quality checks.
- Review the diff for accidental duplication, leaked responsibilities, missing validation/authorization, and hidden environment assumptions.

Evidence packet
Save the command/request used, expected result, actual result, one failure reproduction, the fix, and a short explanation of why the final responsibility belongs where it does. This packet is more valuable than a screenshot of a green page because it demonstrates repeatable engineering reasoning.

Stretch
Change one requirement after the first implementation. Measure which files must change. If a tiny domain change causes unrelated layers to move, use that evidence to discuss coupling before adding another abstraction.

references.preview:
# Supabase Auth Dashboard Setup - TaskFlow Phase 17

1. Authentication > Providers > Email: keep Email enabled.
2. Keep email confirmation enabled for the production-style learning flow.
3. Authentication > URL Configuration:
   - Site URL: http://localhost:3000 for local development.
   - Add production/staging redirect URLs before deployment.
4. Authentication > Email Templates > Confirm signup:

   Replace the confirmation link target with:

   {{ .SiteURL }}/auth/confirm?token_hash={{ .TokenHash }}&type=email

5. Never place a service-role or secret API key in NEXT_PUBLIC_* variables.
6. Phase 17 uses the project's Publishable key in the browser and SSR clients.

# Phase 17 Test Matrix

- Unauthenticated GET /account -> redirected to /login.
- Unauthenticated GET /tasks -> redirected to /login.
- Sign up with valid email/password and email confirmation enabled -> no immediate session; message asks user to check email.
- Confirmation link -> /auth/confirm verifies token_hash and stores cookie-backed session.
- Confirmed user signs in -> redirected to /account.
- Refresh /account -> remains signed in.
- Wait/force access-token refresh path -> proxy keeps cookies synchronized.
- Sign out -> current browser session cookies cleared and /account redirects to /login.
- Invalid confirmation link -> /auth/error.
- Server protection uses getClaims(), not getSession().user.
- Service-role/secret key is absent from browser code and NEXT_PUBLIC_* variables.
